entries.title: Psalms 85:1
segments:
. On the ground of former mercies, the Psalmist prays for renewed blessings, and, confidently expecting them, rejoices. 
 
    1. captivity--not necessarily the Babylonian, but any great evil (

entries.title: Psalms 85:3
segments: 3. To turn from the "fierceness," implies that He was reconcilable, though

entries.title: Psalms 85:4
segments: 4-7. having still occasion for the anger which is deprecated.

entries.title: Psalms 85:8
segments: 8. He is confident God will favor His penitent people (

entries.title: Psalms 85:9
segments: 9. They are here termed "them that fear him"; and grace produces glory (

entries.title: Psalms 85:10
segments: 10. God's promises of "mercy" will be verified by His "truth" (compare
); and the "work of righteousness" in His holy government shall be "peace" (
). There is an implied contrast with a dispensation under which God's truth sustains His threatened wrath, and His righteousness inflicts misery on the wicked.

entries.title: Psalms 85:11
segments: 11. Earth and heaven shall abound with the blessings of this government;

entries.title: Psalms 85:12
segments: 12, 13. and, under this, the deserted land shall be productive, and men be "set," or guided in God's holy ways. Doubtless, in this description of God's returning favor, the writer had in view that more glorious period, when Christ shall establish His government on God's reconciled justice and abounding mercy.
